rows.R: Protocol pp. 8, 18 specify 1000 mg omega-3 per capsule and p. 23 an intended EPA+DHA dose of 1.0 g/day; article pp. 1-2 and eAppendix 2 (supp3 p. 4) report 1412 mg EPA+DHA/day. 1412/1000 = 141%, outside the protocol's 90%-125% manufacturing allowance (p. 20). Not explained in the supplied documents.
rows.evidence: Main PDF pp. 1-2 (text); joi190007supp3 p. 4 (text); joi190007supp1 pp. 8, 18, 20, 23 (text). Card C001 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Same quantity (daily EPA+DHA in the single omega-3 capsule) is stated as 1.0 g/day in the protocol and 1412 mg/day in the report. Ratio 1412/1000 = 1.412, beyond the protocol's 125% upper deviation. The protocol's 'EPA > 700 mg, DHA > 100 mg' are lower bounds and do not by themselves conflict with 1412 mg, but the explicit 1.0 g/day target and 1000 mg/capsule do. This is a planned-versus-reported difference in the delivered intervention dose; I describe it as substantive because the reported exposure differs by about 40% from the planned one. No amendment or formulation document reconciling the two is supplied.

rows.R: Protocol v7 §10.1 (p. 43) plans Kaplan-Meier/log-rank and Cox PH as the primary time-to-event analysis plus mixed models for MDD onset and IDS; the SAP (pp. 3-4) and the article (pp. 4, 6) use logistic regression for cumulative MDD with Cox only secondary/post hoc. KM/log-rank and mixed-model MDD results are not reported. Report matches the undated SAP, so plan sequence is unclear.
rows.evidence: joi190007supp1 p. 43 (text); joi190007supp2 pp. 2-4 (text); main pp. 1, 4, 6, 8 (text); searched all report PDFs for Kaplan, log-rank, mixed model (no hits in report). Card C002 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Protocol (version 7, July 2017, 'with final amendments') specifies KM, log-rank and Cox PH for time to MDD and repeated-measures mixed models for MDD and IDS as the primary analysis. The SAP specifies logistic regression on cumulative 12-month MDD as primary and Cox as secondary. The article follows the SAP (logistic regression primary; Cox HR reported but labeled post hoc). The difference between protocol and report is real, but the SAP is undated and the article cites it, so the change may reflect a later plan version; I therefore code version_timing rather than substantive_difference.

rows.R: Figure 1 (main p. 3, rendered) labels 1451 online exclusions 'BMI <15 or >40', while eAppendix 1 (supp3 p. 3) states the online tool used BMI 25-40, as do the abstract and Methods. The lower cutoff of 15 contradicts 25; the later 18 telephone exclusions for BMI <25 leave open which cutoff was applied online.
rows.evidence: Main p. 3 Figure 1 (rendered PNG, 110 dpi), main pp. 1-2 (text); joi190007supp3 p. 3 (text); protocol p. 16. Flow sums checked. Card C003 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Flow arithmetic reconciles: 1451+623+591+566+268+220+11 = 3730; 5965-3730 = 2235; 2235-462 = 1773; telephone exclusions sum to 523; 1773-523 = 1250; 1250-225 = 1025. The only discrepancy is the label: online exclusion criterion printed as BMI <15 or >40 vs the stated online inclusion criterion BMI 25-40. Either the figure label is a typographic error (most likely <25) or the online screen used a looser cutoff than reported; the 18 later BMI <25 exclusions are compatible with either. The eligibility of the randomized population (BMI 25-40) is stated consistently elsewhere, so I rate it minor presentation with unlikely downstream impact.

rows.R: Main p. 4: '392 participants (196 in each of the 4 possible intervention combinations)'; 4 x 196 = 784, not 392. power.prop.test(p1=.20, p2=.30, power=.90) gives n = 391.9 per group, so 392 is the size of each main-effect arm (2 cells x 196), not the total. 196/0.78 = 251.3, consistent with 250 per cell.
rows.evidence: Main p. 4 Sample Size (text). R: power.prop.test, script R/p0556.R. Card C004 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Recomputed in R: power.prop.test(p1 = 0.2, p2 = 0.3, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.9) gives n = 391.95 per group. Thus 392 is the per-group requirement for each main-effect comparison, which in a 2x2 factorial is two cells of 196. The sentence calls 392 the total of four cells of 196 (= 784). The attrition step 196/(1-0.22) = 251.3 is consistent with 250 per combination and the final 1025 randomized. The intended design is recoverable, so the error is a wording/arithmetic slip of minor presentational importance.

rows.R: Protocol §4.4 (pp. 16-17): control 30% vs intervention 15%, additive interaction, 180 per group, 20% dropout, 250 per arm. Article p. 4: 30% vs 20% (33% reduction), main effects, 196 per cell, 22% attrition, 250 per cell. Event-rate assumption and target contrast differ; final 250 per arm agrees.
rows.evidence: joi190007supp1 pp. 16-17 (text); main p. 4 (text). R power.prop.test for both assumption sets (R/p0556.R). Card C005 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Planned assumptions: 30% vs 15%, interaction-based calculation, 180 per group, 20% drop-out (180/0.8 = 225, rounded up to 250). Reported: 30% vs 20%, main-effect calculation, 196 per cell, 22% attrition (196/0.78 = 251). For reference, power.prop.test(p1 = .15, p2 = .30, power = .90) gives 160.8 per group and (p1 = .20, p2 = .30) gives 391.9 per group. The anticipated effect size and the contrast powered differ between plan and report, although alpha, power and the final 250 per arm agree. The report does not mention the change.

rows.R: Protocol v7 lists IDS with MDD incidence under main study parameters/endpoints (pp. 8-9, 28 §8.1.1; p. 43 §10.1); SAP p. 2 and article p. 4 make IDS secondary. GAD-7 and EQ-5D are protocol secondary, SAP 'Other', article secondary. Report follows the SAP for IDS; SAP is undated.
rows.evidence: joi190007supp1 pp. 8-9, 28, 43 (text); joi190007supp2 p. 2 (text); main p. 4 and Table 3 p. 8 (text). Card C006 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: IDS status changes from main/primary endpoint (protocol) to secondary (SAP and article). GAD-7 and utility are 'Other' in the SAP but secondary in the protocol and article; the SAP 'Other' heading may be organizational. The status change is real between protocol and report, but the report matches the SAP, whose date relative to protocol v7 cannot be established from the supplied material. Coded version_timing.

rows.R: Cox time-to-MDD is planned in protocol §10.1 (as primary) and SAP p. 4 (secondary), and effect modification by site and MDD history in SAP pp. 4-5, yet article p. 4 and Table 2 call Cox 'post hoc' and p. 8 calls the site/history/baseline moderation analyses 'post hoc'. Analyses were done; only their prespecification status is mislabeled.
rows.evidence: joi190007supp1 pp. 43-44; joi190007supp2 pp. 4-5; main pp. 4, 6-8; joi190007supp3 pp. 18-20 (all text). Card C007 read after judging; agrees on the difference.
rows.rationale: Article Methods (p. 4) say Cox was used 'as post hoc analysis' and Table 2 heads the HR results 'Post Hoc Outcome'. Article Methods treat site/history effect modification as planned and only baseline severity as post hoc, but Results (p. 8) call all three moderation analyses post hoc. Both plan documents contain Cox and site/history effect modification. The difference is in the stated status, not in the conduct; I describe it as a labelling difference. A reader would underestimate the prespecification of these analyses.

rows.R: SAP p. 4 plans a RERI (additive interaction) sensitivity analysis for the primary outcome with likelihood-based CIs. No RERI or additive-interaction result appears in the article or eSupplement (text search for RERI/additive/relative excess: no hits in report PDFs). Only multiplicative OR/HR interactions are reported.
rows.evidence: joi190007supp2 p. 4 (text); main pp. 4, 6-7; joi190007supp3 pp. 18-22 (text); grep over all report PDFs. Card C008 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: A planned primary-outcome sensitivity analysis on the additive scale is absent from all supplied report documents. The multiplicative interaction OR 0.93 (P = .48) is a different estimand. Not disclosed as omitted.

rows.R: SAP p. 5 commits to reported sensitivity analyses for the MAR assumption of the primary-outcome multiple imputation. The report's only no-imputation sensitivity (eAppendix 11, supp3 p. 21) covers secondary continuous outcomes; CACE (p. 22) uses MI and is not a missingness sensitivity. No primary-MDD missing-data sensitivity found.
rows.evidence: joi190007supp2 p. 5 (text); main pp. 4, 6, 8; joi190007supp3 pp. 21-22 (text); grep for complete case/MNAR (none). Card C009 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Primary MDD has 239 (23%) participants who dropped out before 12 months or onset (main p. 6). The SAP states that, because MAR cannot be validated, sensitivity analyses will be conducted and reported. The report gives no complete-case, MNAR or other sensitivity analysis for the primary outcome. The SAP sentence could be read as general rather than primary-specific, but it sits in the primary-outcome MI paragraph.

rows.R: eAppendix 7 (supp3 p. 15) defines CACE as ITT effect / complier proportion. ITT ORs (Table 2): supplements 1.06, therapy 0.93; CACE ORs (p. 22): 0.84 and 0.78. Any such ratio keeps the ITT direction, yet supplement CACE reverses it (crude ITT RD +0.6 pp). Therapy: exp(log 0.93/0.713) = 0.90, not 0.78. Values cannot be reproduced from the stated method.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 6, 8 (text); joi190007supp3 pp. 14-16, 22 (text). R computation in R/p0556.R. Card C010 read after judging; it frames this as an unclear mapping; I go further on the direction reversal.
rows.rationale: Under the stated IV logic (exclusion restriction, no defiers) the complier effect equals ITT effect / compliance proportion on the risk-difference scale and must share the ITT sign. Crude ITT RDs: supplements 54/512 - 51/513 = +0.0061; therapy 48/512 - 57/513 = -0.0174. ITT OR for supplements is 1.06 (>1), but its CACE OR is 0.84 (<1): a direction reversal the stated estimator cannot produce on any scale. For therapy, log-scale ratio with compliance about 0.713 (71.9% and 70.7%, supp3 p. 16) gives exp(log(0.93)/0.713) = 0.903 (or 0.816 if the effect-coded OR is first converted to a between-arm OR, 0.93^2). Neither gives 0.78. A logistic SEM with latent compliance, covariates and MI can depart from a simple ratio, which is why I code probable rather than confirmed. Substantive because the therapy CACE (OR 0.78, 0.64-0.95) is the only nominally significant primary-outcome finding and is used in the Results and Discussion.

rows.R: eAppendix 10 Table B (supp3 p. 19, rendered): Spain 0.107 (-0.424 to 0.520), UK 0.117 (-0.371 to 0.638), Germany 0.058 (-0.401 to 0.606) are not centered (midpoints 0.048, 0.134, 0.102) while all six other rows are. 2B-L gives 0.638, 0.605, 0.517: the upper limits appear rotated among the three site rows.
rows.evidence: joi190007supp3 p. 19 (text and rendered PNG 130 dpi). R: midpoints, SEs and Wald P values (R/p0556.R). Card C011 read after judging; agrees, and its 2B-L diagnostic supports the row-rotation reading.
rows.rationale: Linear-model coefficients with Wald CIs are symmetric. Midpoints: Supplements -0.107, F-BA -0.054, History -0.3175, GAD 0.4645, interactions -0.016 and 0.062, all matching B. Site rows: midpoints 0.048, 0.1335, 0.1025 vs B 0.107, 0.117, 0.058. Implied upper limits 2B-L: Spain 0.638, UK 0.605, Germany 0.517, which match the printed UK, Germany and Spain upper limits (0.638, 0.606, 0.520) in rotated order, indicating a transcription error. Wald P values from B and CI-derived SE: 0.657, 0.649, 0.821 vs printed 0.694, 0.637, 0.804. These are adjustment covariates in a supplementary moderation model; no conclusion depends on them.

rows.R: Protocol §3.9.8 (p. 12): relapse criterion 2 is HAM-D >=18 AND a 5-point increase from RCT entry (preferably sustained 1 week). Article p. 4 lists HDRS >=18 alone. Primary composite definition differs as printed; the extra condition matters only for participants entering near 13-15, so the practical effect is probably small.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 1, 4, 6-7 incl. Table 3 (text); joi190079supp1 p. 12 (text). Card C001 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The printed primary-outcome rule in the report omits the conjunctive +5-point increase and the 'preferably 1 week' persistence qualifiers in the plan. Entry HDRS was <=10 (remission) or 11-15 (near remission); mean 5.3 (SD 3.6) at randomization (Table 2), so for most participants a score >=18 implies an increase >=5, but a near-remission participant at 14-15 could reach 18 with an increase <5. Whether the article abbreviates an unchanged operational rule cannot be determined. The difference concerns the primary outcome definition, so I describe it as substantive while noting its likely small practical effect.

rows.R: Protocol p. 10 names HOMA insulin resistance as the primary glycemic measure, a separate BMI alternative analysis and a secondary weight analysis accounting for depression-related weight loss; p. 16 plans an Intent-to-Attend attrition model. None appears in the article or eFigures (text search: no HOMA/insulin/BMI/intent hits). Article limits scope to Aims 1-2 but these belong to Aim 2.
rows.evidence: joi190079supp1 pp. 10, 14, 16 (text); main pp. 1-9 and joi190079supp2 pp. 1-10 (text, grep). Card C002 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The report gives glucose and HbA1c but not HOMA, which the protocol designates the primary glycemic measure; premorbid weight is used only descriptively and for the adverse weight-change threshold; pattern-mixture models are reported but the Intent-to-Attend comparison is not; no BMI model. The HOMA omission is the most consequential. The candidate bundles four omissions of differing weight; collectively they are planned key-secondary analyses not reported.

rows.R: Protocol p. 15 defines phase-specific adverse-event incidence among participants not meeting the criterion at acute-phase baseline (plus week-8-onward reporting); article p. 4 defines UKU adverse effects and incident akathisia relative to RCT baseline. Reference epoch for incidence differs.
rows.evidence: joi190079supp1 p. 15 (text); main pp. 2-4, 7 (text). Card C003 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Acute-phase baseline precedes 12-20 weeks of open-label olanzapine; RCT baseline follows it. Defining incidence from RCT baseline changes which participants are at risk and which events count (e.g., weight gain or akathisia acquired during open-label treatment). The plan also asked for week-8-onward rates, which are not reported. The report's choice is reasonable for a randomized comparison but differs from the plan.

rows.R: Protocol pp. 14, 16: safety (H2) models classify participants 'based on medications taken during protocolized treatment' (regulatory approach). Article p. 4: 'Analyses included all randomized participants'; eFigures 1-8 titles say 'Randomized Groups'. Figure 1 shows 5 + 2 participants not treated as randomized (59+5 = 64; 60+2 = 62).
rows.evidence: joi190079supp1 pp. 14, 16 (text); main pp. 3-4, 7-8 (text); joi190079supp2 pp. 1-9 (text). Card C004 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Planned as-treated classification for weight/metabolic safety analyses versus reported analysis by randomized group. With 7 participants who did not receive treatment as randomized (Figure 1: olanzapine arm 3 discontinued and 2 switched to open-label olanzapine; placebo arm 1 discontinued and 1 switched), the classification rule could change group membership for a few participants. The report does not mention the planned rule.

rows.R: Protocol p. 14 builds exclusion of metabolic data after a new/changed hyperlipidemia treatment into the H2 mixed model; article pp. 5, 7 present the exclusion (statins 6+6 = 12, hypoglycemics 2+1 = 3) as a post hoc sensitivity analysis, with the main models including all data. Planned primary rule became a sensitivity analysis and is labeled post hoc.
rows.evidence: joi190079supp1 p. 14 (text); main pp. 1, 5, 7 (text). Card C005 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The plan's principal H2 model excludes post-treatment-change lipid data; the report's principal estimates appear to include them, and the excluding analysis is described as post hoc with only 'qualitatively similar' results and no estimates. The report's wording could mean only the hypoglycemic extension was post hoc, but the article contrasts the sensitivity analyses with 'analyses that included all participants'. Retained as a difference in the role of a planned analysis rule.

rows.R: Original and final SAP (supp3 pp. 17, 58) promise relative risks in each anatomical stratum from relative-risk regression. Article (pp. 1, 4-6, Table 2) and eSupplement give only ORs and risk differences for the subgroups. Counts allow crude RRs (58/78 vs 42/76: 1.35; 6/18 vs 14/22: 0.52), so the omission is of a planned effect measure, not of the subgroup result.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp3 pp. 17, 57-58 (text); main pp. 1, 4-6 Table 2 (text); joi190092supp1 p. 1 contents. R computation in R/p12618.R. Card C001 read after judging; agrees on absence.
rows.rationale: The prespecified anatomical subgroup analysis is reported (interaction P = .004; stratum ORs and RDs with CIs). The SAP sentence 'We will also report relative risks in each substratum, using relative risk regression' is not honored anywhere in the supplied report. Because the stratum counts are printed, a reader can derive crude RRs (computed: 1.35 and 0.52), although not model-based ones with site random effects. The difference is real but of limited consequence, so I describe it as minor.

rows.R: Final protocol v4.5 §2.5.1 (supp2 p. 80, scanned; OCR) defines success to include 'no periocular or intravitreal corticosteroid injections after the first 90 days'. Article p. 3 omits this component and calls late injections protocol deviations (4 + 4 patients, p. 6); how these 8 were scored is not stated. Original protocol (p. 15, OCR) lacks the component, so the report matches the earlier definition.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp2 pp. 15, 80, 81 (image-only pages, RapidOCR 300 dpi); joi190092supp3 p. 70 §3.5.1 (text); main pp. 3, 4, 6 (text). Card C002 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Primary composite in the final protocol: controlled inflammation, prednisone <=7.5 mg, <=2 drops, no injections after day 90, no failure for safety/tolerability/futility. Article: the same without the injection criterion; late injections described only as deviations. The final SAP §3.5.1 treats late injections in a sensitivity analysis (status at time of injection), which is not reported either (see C003). Eight patients received late injections, so the definition could affect primary counts. The version sequence is clear (original 2012, final 2017) and the report follows neither the final definition nor states its rule.

rows.R: Final SAP §3.5 (supp3 pp. 68-69) commits to reporting four missing-data approaches (regression MI, longitudinal GLMM, assigned success/failure, complete case) plus hot-deck MI; §3.3.1 a tipping-point analysis; §3.5.1 an injection-time sensitivity. Article reports complete case (primary) and one MI sensitivity only (p. 7). The rest are absent.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp3 pp. 22, 28-29, 62, 68-70, 81 (text, pp. 67-68 rendered); main pp. 4, 6-7 Figure 2 (text); joi190092supp1 contents. Card C003 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The SAP says 'We propose to report the results from all of the following methods' and designates complete case as primary on DSMB advice, the others supplementary. Reported: complete-case OR 1.50 (0.81-2.81) and MI OR 1.4 (0.8-2.4), plus site/country and per-protocol sensitivities. Not reported: GLMM, best/worst assignment, tipping point, hot-deck MI, injection-time reclassification. These are planned robustness analyses of the primary endpoint.

rows.R: Final SAP §3.2.3 (supp3 pp. 61-62, 66): Aim 2 primary analysis is logistic regression with treatment group and reason for first-drug failure, plus success probabilities with 95% CIs for each rescue group. Article Table 2 footnote b and p. 4 use the primary model (treatment fixed, site random) for 20/29 vs 7/20; no failure-reason term and no per-group CIs are reported.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp3 pp. 21, 25, 61-62, 66-68 (text); main pp. 4, 6-7 (text); joi190092supp1 p. 1. Card C004 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Reported switching comparison: 20/29 (69%) vs 7/20 (35%), RD 34.2% (6.6% to 52.6%), OR 4.17 (1.32-13.16), P = .02; the text gives OR 4.2 (1.3-13.2), consistent after rounding. The SAP calls the per-group success estimates with CIs 'a central goal of the trial' to be presented regardless of the test, and the primary model includes failure reason. Neither element is reported. Proportions are printed, so crude CIs could be derived, but the planned adjusted model is absent.

rows.R: Main p. 6/Table 2: missed doses 4.6% (SD 1.0) vs 4.3% (SD 0.5), Welch t test P = .87. Welch with n = 96/98: t = 2.63, df = 139, P = .009 (n = 107/109: P = .006). P = .87 would need SDs of about 12.5 points. Summary statistics and P value are incompatible; one is misreported. The 0.3-point difference is clinically trivial either way.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 4, 6 Table 2, 7 Figure 2 (text). R Welch computation in R/p12618.R. Card C005 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Welch t: se = sqrt(1.0^2/96 + 0.5^2/98) = 0.1139; t = 0.3/0.1139 = 2.63; df = 139.1; P = 0.0094. Allowing rounding of inputs (card) P stays below about 0.10. With equal SDs, P = .87 requires SD near 12.5; treating printed SDs as SEs gives P about .79. SDs of 0.5-1.0 percentage points for a per-patient proportion of missed doses are implausibly small, so the dispersion values are the more likely error. The inference that adherence was similar is unaffected in practical terms (0.3-point difference), so minor presentation; downstream impact unlikely beyond extraction of these SDs.

rows.R: SAP §4.1 (supp3 pp. 31, 71): per-protocol population excludes major protocol deviations and noncompliance <50% of study drug received. Article p. 6 and Figure 2 (p. 7) define the per-protocol model as patients who missed <20% of doses (>80% received), n = 184, with no deviation criterion.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp3 pp. 31, 71-72 (text); main pp. 6-7 Figure 2 (text). Card C006 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Planned cutoff >=50% received vs reported >80% received; the major-deviation exclusion (including late injections, out-of-window visits) is not applied in the reported per-protocol model. Figure 2: 61/90 vs 54/94, OR 1.56 (0.84-2.96). The population definition for this sensitivity analysis differs from the plan.

rows.R: eTable 9 (supp1 p. 15, rendered): serious systemic diarrhea, mycophenolate column (N = 20) shows 1 (3.4). 1/20 = 5.0%; 1/29 = 3.4% (the methotrexate column N). Other entries in the same column use N = 20 (e.g., allergic reaction 1 (5.0)). Percentage computed with wrong denominator.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp1 pp. 15-16 (text and rendered PNG 120 dpi). Card C007 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: 1/20 = 0.050; 1/29 = 0.0345. All other mycophenolate-column percentages in eTable 9 use N = 20 (3 (15.0), 4 (20.0), 1 (5.0)). The count (1) is clear, so the error is presentational.

rows.R: SAP availability table (supp3 pp. 26, 67, rendered) gives B/A = 58.3 and A/B = 38.9, but the power table headings put 58 under 'Drug A, then Drug B' and the 0.42 rescue success under 'Drug B in patients failing Drug A'. Text defines n1 = 58 and p1 = 0.42 consistently, so the power values reproduce (87%, 80%, 83%...); headings are swapped. Also 58/38 ignore the stated r2 = 0.95 (55.4/36.9 gives 86%).
rows.evidence: joi190092supp3 pp. 25-27 (original SAP) and 66-68 (final SAP; pp. 67-68 rendered at 110 dpi). R power recomputation in R/p12618.R. Card C008 read after judging; it frames the issue as sequence labels; I agree and add the r2 point.
rows.rationale: n_j = N0 r1 (1-s_j) r2: 108 x 0.9 x 0.6 = 58.32 (x 0.95 = 55.40); 108 x 0.9 x 0.4 = 38.88 (x 0.95 = 36.94). Recomputed Chao formula power: 58/38 with 0.42 vs 0.15 = 0.874; 0.42 vs 0.17 = 0.802; 0.15 vs 0.42 = 0.829; 58/76 = 0.941; 116/38 = 0.955; 40/40 = 0.800; 0.40 vs 0.15 = 0.823 (printed 80%); with 55.4/36.9 = 0.861. The sequence headings of the power table contradict the availability table and the p0/p1 definitions, but the computation itself pairs the larger group with 0.42 as the text intends. Real internal inconsistency in the plan, with little effect on the design.

rows.R: SAP (supp3 pp. 27, 67) says '80% power to detect a difference of 17% if the probability of success with mycophenolate mofetil is 0.42'; the table row 0.42 vs 0.17 gives 80% (recomputed 0.802) and the summary says a 25% difference. 0.42 - 0.17 = 0.25. A literal 17-point difference (0.42 vs 0.25) gives 43% power. '17%' is the comparator probability, not the difference.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp3 pp. 26-27 and 67-68 (text; pp. 67-68 rendered). R power computation in R/p12618.R. Card C009 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Power(58, 38, 0.42, 0.17) = 0.802; power(58, 38, 0.42, 0.25) = 0.43 (card value; consistent with formula). The sentence mislabels the detectable difference; the table and bold summary state the intended 25-point difference, so the meaning is recoverable.

rows.R: Final protocol Table 3 (supp2 p. 81, scanned; OCR): serious lab events AST/ALT >=5x ULN, leukocytes <=1000/uL, hemoglobin <6.5; nonserious Hb >=6.5 to <9. Report Table 3 (p. 8) and eTable 1 (supp1 p. 5): AST/ALT >5x, leukocytes <1000, Hb >6.5 to <9. Only exact boundary values are treated differently; cutoffs otherwise agree.
rows.evidence: joi190092supp2 pp. 80-81, 136 (image-only; RapidOCR 300 dpi, confidence >=0.91 on table rows); main pp. 3, 6, 8 (text); joi190092supp1 p. 5 (text). Card C010 read after judging; agrees and notes the original protocol used >5x.
rows.rationale: Inclusive vs strict inequalities at 5x ULN, 1000/uL and 6.5 g/dL; the report's partitions also leave exact values (e.g., Hb = 6.5, leukocytes = 1000) unclassified. These feed the safety-failure component of the primary outcome, but only measurements exactly at the boundary are affected; all 5 drug-related serious events were liver tests. A real but minor difference.

rows.R: Protocol (supp2 p. 3): 'Each non-surgical patient will be matched ... to five (5) surgical patients'; article (pp. 1, 3-4): each surgical patient matched to 5 nonsurgical (2287 and 11 435; 11 435/2287 = 5.0). The protocol's own sensitivity section (p. 6) refers to reporting the 1:5 dataset, so the plan sentence reads as transposed wording; the conduct is clear.
rows.evidence: joi190103supp2 pp. 3, 6, 7 (text); main pp. 1, 3-4 incl. Figure 1 (text). Card C001 read after judging; agrees on the literal difference.
rows.rationale: The literal plan sentence specifies a 5:1 surgical:control allocation, which would be infeasible with 2287 surgical and 39 267 eligible controls; the plan's sensitivity text (ratios 1:1, 1:5, 1:10; results reported from 1:5) and the report agree on 1 surgical : 5 controls. I therefore describe this as a wording slip in the plan rather than a change of design. Note also that the protocol is dated January 6, 2019, after data closure (December 31, 2018).

rows.R: Table 2 (main p. 7): ARD = control minus surgery 8-y risk reproduces for primary, secondary and mortality (16.9, 10.6, 7.8) but not for HF (18.9-6.8 = 12.1 vs 12.9), CAD (3.7 vs 4.2), cerebrovascular (1.5 vs 1.8), nephropathy (10.2 vs 11.1) or AF (5.7 vs 6.5); eTable 5 confirms the group risks. Gaps 0.3-0.9 points exceed rounding. The five rows are exactly those with outcome-specific risk sets.
rows.evidence: Main p. 7 Table 2, p. 4 methods (text); joi190103supp1 p. 7 eTable 5 (text). R subtraction in R/p14231.R. Card C002 read after judging; agrees; the risk-set pattern is my addition.
rows.rationale: Subtraction of displayed one-decimal risks can differ from the true difference by at most 0.1 point; observed gaps are 0.8, 0.5, 0.3, 0.9 and 0.8. The three matching rows use the full matched cohort (2287/11 435 at risk) while the five non-matching rows use reduced risk sets that exclude patients with prior history of that outcome (e.g., HF 2049/10 093), which suggests the ARDs were computed on a different population or by a different estimator than the displayed risks. Whatever the mechanism, the table pairs ARDs with risks that do not yield them. ARDs are headline extractable quantities (e.g., HF 12.9 vs 12.1), so substantive with direct extraction impact.

rows.R: Cerebrovascular row: unadjusted 8-year KM ARD 1.8 (bootstrap 95% CI -0.03 to 3.4) vs adjusted Cox HR 0.67 (0.48-0.94), P = .02 (P implied by HR CI = .0195). Different estimands and models (fixed-time unadjusted risk difference vs adjusted hazard ratio over follow-up); differing null readings are not a contradiction.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 4, 6-8 Table 2 and Figure 3D (text); joi190103supp1 p. 9 eTable 6. R p_from_ci in R/p14231.R. Card C003 read after judging; its own alternative interpretation agrees.
rows.rationale: Table 2 footnotes a and b attribute the CI to bootstrap of the 8-year KM difference and the P value to the adjusted Cox model. The HR, CI and P are mutually consistent (recomputed P = 0.0195). A fixed-horizon unadjusted risk difference with an interval including 0 can coexist with a significant adjusted HR. The ARD point value itself belongs to the C002 problem (subtraction gives 1.5).

rows.R: Protocol p. 4 lists CAD 'Other' codes (ICD9 411.X, 411.X AND 414.X) with no diagnosis-position condition; report eTable 1 (supp1 p. 2, rendered) bolds 411.X and 414.X with footnote 'must be a primary diagnosis'. The protocol also says 'see eTable 1 for diagnosis codes/definitions', so the plan may already have carried the restriction; the plan's eTable is not supplied.
rows.evidence: joi190103supp2 p. 4 (rendered PNG 130 dpi), p. 7; joi190103supp1 p. 2 eTable 1 (rendered PNG 130 dpi); main pp. 2, 7. Card C004 read after judging; agrees, including the incorporation-by-reference caveat.
rows.rationale: The printed inline plan list and the report's eTable 1 differ in a primary-component operational criterion (primary-diagnosis requirement). Because the plan explicitly defers to an eTable 1 that may be the same table, whether the restriction was planned cannot be established. Retained as a printed difference with indeterminate interpretation.

rows.R: Protocol p. 4 lists AF ICD-10 codes i48.0, i48.2, i48.91; report eTable 1 (supp1 p. 2, rendered) lists i48.0, i48.1, i48.2, i48.91. Persistent AF (i48.1) is added to a component of the primary composite. The protocol refers to eTable 1, so the plan's governing list is uncertain, but the printed lists differ.
rows.evidence: joi190103supp2 p. 4 (rendered), p. 7; joi190103supp1 p. 2 (rendered); main pp. 2, 7. Card C005 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Set difference report minus plan = {i48.1}; plan minus report = empty. Adding a code broadens the AF outcome and the extended-MACE composite. Same caveat as C004 about incorporation of eTable 1 by reference; I code substantive_difference because the explicit code list for an outcome component differs.

rows.R: Protocol p. 6: no adjustment for multiple comparisons of secondary end points; 95% CIs reported. Report eTable 8 (supp1 p. 12, rendered) gives Bonferroni-corrected 98.8% CIs for weight, HbA1c, nutritional and medication changes at 1, 2, 5, 8 years. The main text (p. 7, Figure 4) labels the same 8-year HbA1c interval (1.0-1.2) as 95%.
rows.evidence: joi190103supp2 pp. 6-7 (text); joi190103supp1 p. 12 eTable 8 (rendered PNG 130 dpi); main pp. 4, 7, Figure 4 (text). Card C006 read after judging; agrees; the 95%/98.8% labelling clash in the main text is my addition.
rows.rationale: 1 - 0.05/4 = 0.9875, printed 98.8%, consistent with a four-time-point Bonferroni family. The plan's no-adjustment statement may have been intended only for the vascular secondary outcomes, but it does not define a separate corrected family. Additionally, the report labels the 8-year HbA1c difference 1.1% (95% CI 1.0-1.2) in the main text and -1.1 (98.8% CI -1.2 to -1.0) in eTable 8; weight 20.3 (95% CI 20.1-20.6) vs -20.3 (98.8% CI -20.6 to -20.0). Both cannot carry those coverage levels; noted here as an observation outside the candidate.

rows.R: eTable 8 year-5 hemoglobin -0.1 (98.8% CI -0.2, 0), P <.001. With one-decimal display, e.g. estimate -0.15, limits -0.25 and -0.05 print as -0.1 (-0.2, 0) [-0.05 rounds to -0.0/0]; then SE = 0.1/2.51 = 0.040, z = 3.8, P = .0002. Display precision explains the apparent conflict.
rows.evidence: joi190103supp1 p. 12 eTable 8 (rendered PNG 130 dpi); main p. 4 methods. Calculation shown in rationale. Card C007 read after judging; it lists the same rounding explanation as an alternative.
rows.rationale: 98.8% two-sided z = qnorm(1 - 0.012/2) = 2.51. Values compatible with the printed rounding (estimate in [-0.15, -0.05], lower limit in [-0.25, -0.15], upper limit in [-0.05, 0.05)) include a symmetric interval -0.25 to -0.05 around -0.15, giving z = 0.15/(0.10/2.51) = 3.77 and P = 0.00016 < .001. The printed tuple is therefore attainable without error, and the upper limit is printed with one decimal so '0' is an expected display of a small negative number. Not a reporting error.

rows.R: eTable 12 (supp1 p. 20): rare-outcome E-value 1/HR + sqrt(1/HR(1/HR-1)) reproduces all 7 non-primary rows (e.g., HF 0.38: 4.70; printed 4.69) but not the primary (HR 0.61: 2.66, upper 0.69: 2.26; printed 2.15/1.92). The primary pair matches the common-outcome conversion RR = (1-0.5^sqrt(HR))/(1-0.5^sqrt(1/HR)): 2.16/1.91. Methods differ across rows without statement.
rows.evidence: joi190103supp1 pp. 9, 19-20 (text); main pp. 4, 7, 9; joi190103supp2 p. 7. R E-value computations in R/p14231.R. Card C008 read after judging; it leaves the primary-specific conversion as a possibility; I identify it.
rows.rationale: Recomputed: rare-outcome E-values for HR (upper limit): secondary 2.61 (2.12), mortality 2.78 (2.12), HF 4.70 (3.50), CAD 2.26 (1.56), cerebrovascular 2.35 (1.32), nephropathy 4.44 (3.26), AF 1.88 (1.21), all matching print within rounding of the HR inputs. Primary printed 2.15/1.92 matches the VanderWeele common-outcome square-root conversion (2.16/1.91). Using the common-outcome approach is appropriate where 8-year incidence exceeds about 15% (also secondary 27.6%, mortality 17.8%, HF 18.9%, nephropathy 16.3%), where it would give 2.13, 2.24, 3.29, 3.16. Thus the table mixes methods and overstates robustness for several secondary outcomes. The qualitative conclusion (E-values exceed the HRs of known risk factors, 1.05-1.73) holds under either method, so I rate it minor presentation with possible downstream impact on extracted E-values.

rows.R: Protocol p. 13 and SAP pp. 5, 9-10: primary outcomes are CVD and weight change; dietary scores and nutrient intake are 'other intermediate outcomes'. Interim report (pp. 1-4) makes 12-month er-MedDiet score change the primary end point and weight/waist/risk factors secondary. Disclosed as an interim exploratory analysis (p. 2), but no prospective interim hierarchy is supplied.
rows.evidence: joi190106supp1 pp. 13, 31, 38 (text); joi190106supp2 pp. 2, 5, 9-10 (text); main pp. 1-4 (text). Card C001 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Outcome status changes: weight moves from (co-)primary to secondary; the er-MedDiet score moves from an intermediate outcome to the primary end point of this publication. The report states that it is a preliminary exploratory interim analysis of the ongoing trial, which is disclosure, not a plan document. Retained as a difference with 'disclosed' context.

rows.R: Protocol p. 52 and SAP p. 13: all analyses ITT, each participant remaining in the allocated group. Report (p. 4, Figure 1, eTable 9) excludes 291 randomized participants (53 without baseline FFQ, 238 with implausible energy intake) from all principal analyses, including weight: 3406-134 = 3272, 3468-157 = 3311, total 6583. This dietary-plausibility filter is not a planned membership rule for weight.
rows.evidence: joi190106supp1 p. 52; joi190106supp2 p. 13 (text); main pp. 3-4, Figure 1 (text); joi190106supp3 pp. 23-24 eTable 9 (rendered). Card C002 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Arithmetic reconciles (28+106 = 134; 25+132 = 157; 6874-291 = 6583). The exclusion uses baseline (pre-randomization) dietary data, so it does not break randomization, but it changes the analysis set for weight and waist, whose ascertainment does not depend on the FFQ. The energy limits are 'prespecified' per the report but no supplied plan applies them to the weight outcome.

rows.R: SAP p. 26: 'Main analyses will be based on an intention-to-treat approach with completers only. As sensitivity analysis, ... repeated with multiple imputation.' Report p. 4 reverses this: multiple imputation is principal and completers-only analyses are called 'post hoc sensitivity analyses' (eTables 3-5, 9), although the SAP had planned them as main.
rows.evidence: joi190106supp2 pp. 13, 26 (text); main pp. 3-5 (text); joi190106supp3 pp. 1, 9, 23 (text/rendered). Card C003 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Priority of the two analyses is inverted, and the completers analysis is mislabeled post hoc. Both results are shown (e.g., eTable 9 weight), so the information is available, but the designation of the principal estimate differs from the plan.

rows.R: SAP p. 26: chained equations, 20 imputations, predictors sex, age, smoking, leisure-time PA, baseline BMI and weight, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, family history of CHD, group, second household member, education, for participants lost >=2 years. Report p. 4: iterative MCMC, 8 imputations, predictors sex, age, smoking, education, BMI, PA, group, total energy, baseline value. eTable 9 footnote (p. 24) instead says chained equations, so the report is also internally inconsistent.
rows.evidence: joi190106supp2 p. 26 (text); main p. 4 (text); joi190106supp3 p. 24 eTable 9 footnote (rendered). Card C004 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Method (chained equations vs MCMC), number of imputations (20 vs 8) and predictor set differ. The SAP paragraph may target long-term missing outcomes, but no interim-specific imputation plan is supplied. The difference concerns the analysis method for the principal estimates. Within the report, the risk-factor footnote of eTable 9 (supp3 p. 24) describes imputation by chained equations with a different predictor list (no outcome-specific count), whereas the main text says MCMC with 8 imputations, so the report is itself not consistent about the method used for the weight and risk-factor estimates.

rows.R: SAP pp. 25-26 plan weight models additionally adjusted for center, sex, age, education, smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, family history and PA, plus subgroup analyses (8 factors); protocol p. 52 plans sensitivity excluding second household members. The report gives only crude mixed-model weight results (eTable 9, Figures 3-4); no adjusted, subgroup or household-exclusion analyses.
rows.evidence: joi190106supp1 p. 52; joi190106supp2 pp. 5, 9, 25-26 (text); main pp. 4, 8-10; joi190106supp3 pp. 1, 23-24 (text/rendered). Card C005 read after judging; agrees, including that subgroup applicability to Y1 is uncertain.
rows.rationale: The SAP timeline (p. 9) schedules body-weight change at year 1, and the weight-specific adjustment statement is explicit. Subgroup and household-exclusion analyses may be intended for the final CVD analysis, which limits that part of the candidate, but the adjusted weight model alone is a planned analysis not reported.

rows.R: SAP p. 12: secondary outcomes (27 listed, incl. waist circumference) get nominal 95% CIs plus ancillary Bonferroni-adjusted CIs (1 - 0.05/27 = 99.81%). Report p. 4 states no adjustment for type I error, and the 12-month waist difference -3.3 cm (95% CI -3.6 to -2.9) is shown with nominal CI only. Disclosed in report (p. 4).
rows.evidence: joi190106supp2 pp. 9, 12 (text); main pp. 4, 8 (text); joi190106supp3 p. 23 eTable 9 (rendered). Card C006 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Planned ancillary multiplicity-adjusted intervals are not reported for the named secondary outcome. With P < .001 the adjusted interval would almost certainly still exclude 0, so the practical consequence is small; the difference is in the planned inference output and is disclosed.

rows.R: Main Table 3 (p. 7, rendered 200 dpi): alcohol 12-mo difference -0.2 (95% CI -0.4 to 0.1), P = .01; eTables 5 and 8 give the 12-mo CI as -0.4 to -0.1 and -0.3 to -0.1, so the main-table '0.1' has likely lost its minus sign. The 6-mo rows with an upper limit of 0 and P = .01/.02 can be reproduced by rounding (e.g., -0.18, -0.33 to -0.03 gives P = .02).
rows.evidence: Main p. 7 Table 3 (text and rendered crop at 200 dpi), p. 4; joi190106supp3 p. 15 eTable 5 and p. 22 eTable 8 (rendered 130 dpi). Calculations in rationale. Card C007 read after judging; it registers all four rows; I consider only the main 12-month row a definite conflict.
rows.rationale: A symmetric 95% CI with printed limits -0.4 and 0.1 has midpoint about -0.15 and half-width >= 0.2, so z <= 1.6 and P >= .11, incompatible with P = .01. Crude check from printed summaries: -0.3 vs -0.1 with SD 3.0, n = 3272/3311, gives difference -0.2, SE 0.074, P = .007, consistent with P = .01 and a negative upper limit. For the 6-mo rows, values within display rounding (estimate -0.18, CI -0.33 to -0.03) reproduce P near .02, and the main-table 6-mo P = .01 is attainable only at the rounding boundary. The magnitude (-0.2 percentage points of energy) is clear and clinically negligible; the problem is a sign/typesetting error affecting the extractable CI.

rows.R: eTable 2 (supp3 p. 7, rendered): intervention baseline red wine median (IQR) 33 (0, 29) g/week. A median cannot exceed the upper quartile (33 > 29). Control prints 4 (0, 29), so 33 is probably a typographic error (e.g., 3).
rows.evidence: joi190106supp3 p. 7 eTable 2 (text and rendered PNG 130 dpi). Card C008 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Order statistics require Q1 <= median <= Q3; 33 > 29 even allowing rounding (32.5 > 29.5). The intended value is not recoverable from the table. Descriptive baseline value in a supplement; minor presentation, though an extractor could copy the wrong median.

rows.R: eFigure 2 (supp3 p. 26, rendered): printed percentages inside the bars contradict bar heights: e.g., MUFA:SFA bars about 87% (intervention) and 79% (control) but labels 79% and 86%; fruit about 63/58 vs labels 58/63; vegetables about 65/56 vs 56/64; dessert about 68/60 vs 59/58. Labels look swapped between arms for most pairs, and dessert fits no swap.
rows.evidence: joi190106supp3 p. 26 eFigure 2 (rendered PNG 130 dpi, read visually); main p. 8 text. Card C009 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Bar heights and the main-text statement that favorable changes were more frequent with the intervention agree; the printed numeric labels place the larger value in the control arm for MUFA, MUFA:SFA, fruit, vegetables and meat, and dessert's intervention label (59%) is about 9 points below its bar. The labels are the only numeric values given for these proportions, so an extractor would take reversed or wrong group percentages. Substantive for data extraction; bar heights read visually (+/- 2 points).

rows.R: Protocol v4 p. 30 defines acute respiratory failure with 'Respiratory rate > 25 breaths/min during at least 2 hours'; article p. 4 (and eTable 1, supp2 p. 2) states respiratory rate >25 without the 2-hour duration. This defines a key secondary outcome (29% vs 21%). The article may have condensed the rule; the printed definitions differ.
rows.evidence: joi190108supp1 pp. 25, 30 (text); main pp. 1, 4, 8 Table 2 (text); joi190108supp2 p. 2 (text). Card C001 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Other ARF criteria agree (distress signs, pH <7.35 with PaCO2 >45, FIO2 >=50% or PaO2:FIO2 <=150). Omitting the persistence requirement would allow transient tachypnea to count, which could increase the event count; whether the rule was applied in practice cannot be determined. Coded as a substantive difference in a secondary outcome definition, consistent with how I treated similar omitted conjunctive criteria elsewhere.

rows.R: Protocol §6.2-6.3 (pp. 33-34) plans Cox proportional hazards models with backward selection for reintubation and for ICU, hospital, day-28 and day-90 mortality, expressed as adjusted HRs. The article reports chi-square tests, Kaplan-Meier/log-rank and one logistic model; no Cox model or HR appears in the article or eSupplement.
rows.evidence: joi190108supp1 pp. 33-34 (text); main pp. 1, 4, 6-8 (text); joi190108supp2 pp. 1-9 (text). Card C002 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Planned Cox models are absent from all supplied report documents. The protocol frames them as prognostic (variables associated with reintubation/death at P<.20 entered), so they may not be treatment-effect analyses, but they are planned analyses of the primary and secondary outcomes that are not reported.

rows.R: Protocol p. 33: multivariable logistic model with all variables associated with reintubation at P<.20 plus forced variables, simplified by backward elimination (retain P<.05). Article p. 4: model adjusted for the stratification variable (PaCO2) and baseline variables unbalanced between arms at P<.05 (only chronic lung disease); aOR 0.60 (0.38-0.93). Covariate-selection rules differ; the article says analyses followed a 'predefined statistical analysis plan', which is not supplied.
rows.evidence: joi190108supp1 p. 33 (text); main pp. 4, 6 (Table 1 footnote), 7 (text). Card C003 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Selection by outcome association (P<.20, backward) vs selection by between-arm imbalance (P<.05) are different covariate-selection procedures and would generally yield different models. The article's reference to a predefined SAP may mean a separate document exists, but the supplied plan does not contain the reported rule.

rows.R: Protocol §6.4 (p. 34) plans subgroup analyses of primary and secondary outcomes by PaCO2 (>45 vs <=45), by underlying cardiac or respiratory disease, and by type of weaning test (T-piece vs low pressure support). Only the PaCO2 subgroups are reported (main p. 7, Figure 3; eTables 2-4). The other two families are absent.
rows.evidence: joi190108supp1 p. 34 (text); main pp. 4, 7-8 (text); joi190108supp2 pp. 1, 3-7 (text, pp. 3-4 rendered). Card C004 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: eTable 2 gives baseline counts of chronic cardiac/lung disease and weaning-test type by PaCO2 stratum, but no outcome results by those characteristics. Two planned subgroup families for the primary outcome are not reported and their omission is not explained.

rows.R: eTable 2 (supp2 p. 4, rendered): hypercapnic cells 14/45 (69), 16/59 (73), 20/46 (57), 23/61 (62). Correct percentages are 31.1, 27.1, 43.5, 37.7; each printed value equals 100 minus the correct one (68.9, 72.9, 56.5, 62.3). Counts are correct: they sum with the nonhypercapnic cells to Table 1 totals (65/284, 86/322, 121/288, 114/326).
rows.evidence: joi190108supp2 pp. 3-5 (text; p. 4 rendered at 120 dpi); main p. 6 Table 1. R check of percentages and chi-square (P = .656 uncorrected matches printed .6561). Card C005 read after judging; it notes a possible carry-over from the lung-disease row; the complement pattern explains all four cells.
rows.rationale: 14/45 = 31.1%, 16/59 = 27.1%, 20/46 = 43.5%, 23/61 = 37.7%; printed percentages are their complements. The printed P values match tests on the counts (uncorrected chi-square for cough: P = 0.656), so only the percentages are wrong. Counts allow correct recomputation, so minor presentation; a reader relying on the percentages would invert the prevalence in the hypercapnic subgroup.

rows.R: Original protocol (2010; supp1 pp. 11, 17, 19): primary = 4-year change in urine ACR; secondary = eGFR change and a composite (ACR doubling to >=30, eGFR loss >=12, ESRD, death). Addendum (submitted 3/2015, implemented 2/2016; pp. 31-32 §15b) makes 5-year eGFR change primary and uses a >=40% eGFR loss/ESRD/death composite; the report follows the addendum. Disclosed in report (p. 2).
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 pp. 4, 11, 17, 19, 31-32 (text); main pp. 1-4, 9 Table 3 (text, p. 9 rendered). Card C001 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The change of primary outcome and composite is documented in a dated plan amendment before the end of follow-up (December 2017) and disclosed in the article ('The original primary outcome was change in albuminuria but was modified when the study duration was extended to 5 years in 2016'). Under the review rule that disclosed changes still count as differences, I retain it, noting that the report agrees with the latest supplied plan version.

rows.R: Protocol (pp. 4, 11, 12 Table 1): parent and ancillary eligibility men >=60 y, women >=65 y. Article p. 2: men >=50 y, women >=55 y. The addendum (pp. 31-33) does not revise eligibility. Not disclosed as a change in the article.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 pp. 4, 11-12, 31-33 (text); main p. 2 Study Population (text). Card C002 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The age floor for the enrolled population differs by 10 years from the supplied plan. The change probably reflects the parent VITAL trial's final eligibility, but no supplied document records it for this ancillary study. Population definition difference.

rows.R: Protocol p. 12 (and Table 1) and p. 14: exclude diabetes diagnosed before age 30 and 'first treated with insulin'. Article p. 2: exclude diabetes diagnosed before age 30 'treated with insulin for more than 20 years'. The type 1 diabetes proxy uses a different insulin rule.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 pp. 12, 14 (text); main p. 2 (text). Card C003 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: 'First treated with insulin' and 'insulin for more than 20 years' select different participants (e.g., someone diagnosed at 25 who started insulin first but used it 15 years is excluded under the plan, not under the report). Both target type 1 diabetes; the operational exclusion differs.

rows.R: Protocol §IV.c (p. 14): randomization stratified by 5-year age group, blocks of 8 (two per factorial cell). Article p. 2: blocks of 8 'stratified by age, sex, and race'. Sex and race are added as stratifiers in the report; not mentioned in the addendum.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 pp. 14, 31-33 (text); main p. 2 Interventions (text). Card C004 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Stratification factors are a design element that bears on the analysis (stratified randomization usually implies adjusting for the strata). The report's primary model adjusts for age and sex but not race (see C010). The difference likely reflects the parent trial's final procedure, which the supplied plan does not document.

rows.R: Protocol §VI.c Equation 1 (p. 17): eGFR = 177.6 x SCr^-0.65 x CysC^-0.57 x age^-0.20 x 0.82 (female) x 1.11 (black) [Stevens 2008]. Article p. 3: CKD-EPI creatinine-cystatin C equation (ref 19, 2012). The addendum (p. 32) does not name an estimator. The primary outcome is computed with a different equation.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 pp. 17, 30, 32 (text); main pp. 3, 11 refs (text); joi190122supp2 pp. 2-4 eAppendix (text). Card C005 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The plan's phrase 'using the most precise serologic methods available' could be read as permitting an update, but the plan prints a specific equation. CKD-EPI 2012 and the 2008 equation differ in functional form (spline terms) and yield different eGFR values, so the primary outcome measure differs from the plan. Additionally the eAppendix describes post hoc harmonization of cystatin C, which is disclosed.

rows.R: Article p. 3 and Table 3 footnote a call 'time to doubling of urine ACR to a final ACR >=30 mg/g' a prespecified secondary outcome. The addendum (§15b, p. 32) lists ACR change as continuous plus >=40% eGFR loss and a composite; the original protocol had ACR doubling only inside a different composite. This standalone result (vitamin D HR 1.34, 1.00-1.80, P = .05) lacks a supplied plan basis.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 pp. 17, 32-33 (text); main pp. 3-4, 9 Table 3 (text and rendered PNG 170 dpi). Card C006 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: A 'prespecified' claim not supported by either supplied plan version. It matters because this is the only secondary result at the significance boundary (HR 1.34 [1.00-1.80], P = .05). An unsupplied final SAP could contain it.

rows.R: Protocol §VI.g (p. 19) and addendum §15g (p. 33): adherence sensitivity among participants reporting (continuous) adherence to >=80% of study medications. Article p. 3 and eTables 1, 5, 8: highly adherent defined as using study medications at least two-thirds of the time.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 pp. 19, 33 (text); main pp. 3-4 (text); joi190122supp2 pp. 6, 10, 13 (text). Card C007 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Threshold for the adherent subset changes from >=80% to >=67%, enlarging the sensitivity population. 2/3 is 0.667 vs 0.80. Population for a planned sensitivity analysis differs.

rows.R: Addendum §15c (p. 32): ITT population = all participants who return at least one follow-up biosample, with MI for missing year-5 eGFR. Article p. 3: all randomized participants 'regardless of adherence or follow-up' (n = 1312), imputing outcomes also for the 222 without any follow-up blood sample (1312 - 1090).
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 p. 32 (text); main pp. 3-4, 6 Figure 1, 8 Table 2 (text). Card C008 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The report's primary population is broader than planned: participants with no post-randomization biosample (1312 - 1090 = 222 for blood) are included with fully imputed outcomes. This changes the analysis set and the share of imputed data; results with the complete-case set are similar (eTable 4).

rows.R: Addendum §15c (p. 32): 10 imputed datasets (chained equations) combined by Rubin's rules; article p. 3: M = 20 imputations combined by Rubin's rules. A real but technically minor difference; more imputations reduce Monte Carlo error without changing the estimand.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 p. 32 (text); main pp. 3, 8 Table 2 footnotes (text). Card C009 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: 10 vs 20 imputations. The imputation model description (chained equations using baseline and year-2 data) is not restated in the report. I keep it as a plan-report difference but describe it as minor, because the number of imputations does not alter the target of inference.

rows.R: Addendum Equation 2 (p. 32): eGFR ~ treatment + time + treatment x time + random intercept, with baseline covariates only in sensitivity analyses if imbalance is observed. Article p. 3 and Table 2 footnote a: primary model adds age, sex and their time interactions, and (for eGFR) baseline urine ACR and its time interaction.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 pp. 32-33 (text); main pp. 3, 8 Table 2 (text); joi190122supp2 pp. 9-10 eTables 4-5 (text). Card C010 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Covariate set of the primary model differs from the plan. Adjustment for prognostic covariates in an RCT is defensible and generally increases precision, but it is not what the supplied plan specifies for the primary analysis; no imbalance was reported that would trigger the planned conditional adjustment.

rows.R: Addendum §15f (p. 33) prespecifies vitamin D subgroups by baseline total AND bioavailable 25(OH)D. Article p. 3, Figure 3 and eFigure 2 report total 25(OH)D only; bioavailable 25(OH)D is not reported anywhere in the supplied documents.
rows.evidence: joi190122supp1 p. 33 (text); main pp. 3, 8 Figure 3 (rendered 170 dpi), 9-10 (text; 'bioavailable' appears only in a conflict-of-interest disclosure); joi190122supp2 p. 17 eFigure 1 (text) and p. 18 eFigure 2 (rendered 130 dpi). Card C011 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: A prespecified subgroup analysis is absent without explanation. The article lists the prespecified vitamin D subgroups as race/ethnicity, 25(OH)D, ACR and eGFR, silently dropping the bioavailable measure.

rows.rationale: Conversion: 1 ug vitamin D3 = 40 IU, so 2000 IU = 50 ug. The plan's '40 ug' is a conversion slip; the article reports 2000 IU only. A real plan-internal inconsistency in the dose description, with clear intended meaning.

For a ratio active/placebo of change in ACR, values below 1 favor the active supplement. The labels state the opposite. Because no subgroup estimate excludes 1 and the text does not rely on the figure's direction, I rate it minor presentation, though a reader using the labels would misread direction.

rows.R: Final protocol body (supp1 p. 25) lists de novo cancer as a tertiary outcome, and the change summary (p. 45) records moving it from adverse events to a tertiary outcome in 2012; the final synopsis (p. 19, copied from p. 4) still calls it an adverse event. The outcome's status and analysis population differ from the final plan body.

rows.R: Initial and final SAP method 5c (supp1 pp. 14, 31) and synopsis (p. 19) plan Kaplan-Meier survival curves (ITT). The article (p. 3, Figures 2-3) shows Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard curves; no Kaplan-Meier curve appears in the article or eSupplement (text search). 5-year survival percentages are given in text.
rows.evidence: joi190023supp1 pp. 14, 19, 31, 45 (text); main pp. 1, 3-4, 6-7 (text); joi190023supp2 pp. 1-41 (text search for Kaplan: no hits). Card C002 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Kaplan-Meier survival and Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard describe the same survival experience (S(t) approximately exp(-H(t))), and the reported 5-year RFS and OS percentages are presumably KM estimates. The planned display was replaced by a closely related one; I record the difference but describe it as minor.

rows.R: SAP method 5e (supp1 pp. 14, 31): relapse and safety outcomes evaluated with risk ratios. Article: relapse analyzed with post hoc competing-risk subdistribution HRs (p. 3, Figure 2C, Table 2); safety outcomes given as n (%) only (Table 3). No risk ratio is reported for relapse or any safety outcome. The competing-risk analysis is labeled post hoc (disclosed).
rows.evidence: joi190023supp1 pp. 14, 31 (text); main pp. 3, 6-8 (text); joi190023supp2 searched (no 'risk ratio'). Card C003 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The planned effect measure for relapse (RR) is replaced by a subdistribution HR, and planned RRs for safety outcomes are not reported. Crude RRs could be derived from Table 3 counts, but the planned evaluation is absent. Competing-risk analysis is disclosed as post hoc.

rows.R: Final SAP subgroup analyses (supp1 p. 31; added 2012 per p. 45) define three 25(OH)D groups (<20, 20-40, >40 ng/mL) with interaction testing. The article (pp. 3-4, 7-8) did not analyse the >40 group (n = 5: 4 vs 1) and tested interaction only between low and middle groups. Disclosed and explained in the report.
rows.evidence: joi190023supp1 pp. 31, 45 (text); main pp. 1, 3-5 Table 1, 7 Figure 3 caption, 8 limitations (text). Card C004 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: With 5 participants an analysis would be uninformative, so the omission is reasonable and disclosed, but it changes the planned three-group subgroup structure to a two-group interaction test. Retained as a disclosed difference. Note that the change summary records that the 25(OH)D subgroups were added after trial start (before the first interim analysis), which the article calls prespecified.

rows.R: Table 1 genotype percentages (main p. 5) reproduce with available-case (genotyped) denominators: e.g., FokI 92/245 = 37.6% (printed 38), BsmI 175/231 = 75.8% (76), placebo 119/150 = 79.3% (79). The 251/166 headers are not the denominators, but category sums give them. Fully explained by missing genotype data; one cell (ApaI placebo GT 61/150 = 40.7%, printed 40) is a trivial rounding slip.
rows.evidence: Main p. 5 Table 1 (text). R recomputation of all 42 genotype percentages in R/p2210.R. Card C005 read after judging; it notes the same available-case reconstruction.
rows.rationale: Recomputed with per-locus genotyped totals (vitamin D 230-245, placebo 148-157), all genotype percentages match the print within rounding except ApaI placebo GT (40.7% printed 40%). The apparent mismatch with arm headers reflects missing genotyping, a common and recoverable presentation choice, not an error in the reported values. I therefore exclude it; the unstated missing-genotype counts and the single rounding slip are noted for the coordinator.

rows.R: Table 2 footnote a (main p. 7): 'HR values greater than 1 indicate that vitamin D supplementation was associated with a decreased probability of the outcome.' The text interprets HR <1 as benefit (e.g., relapse sHR 0.44 in the middle subgroup 'significantly lower in the vitamin D group', p. 6; HR 0.76 for relapse or death). The footnote reverses the direction used everywhere else.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 3-4, 6-7 Table 2 and Figures 2-3 (text). Card C006 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Under the stated Cox model with vitamin D vs placebo, HR <1 means lower hazard with vitamin D, as the text and figures (cumulative hazard lower in the vitamin D curves) show. The footnote's statement is the opposite. Because the text makes the direction clear, I rate it minor presentation, but a reader relying on the table footnote alone would invert the interpretation of every Table 2 row.

rows.R: Age-adjusted HR 0.66 (95% CI 0.43-0.99), P = .048 (main p. 6). Nominal Wald P from the CI = .051; allowing display rounding with a symmetric log-scale CI, P ranges .043-.047. The printed .048 differs by <=0.001, which a likelihood-ratio or score P paired with a Wald CI would readily explain. Not a meaningful inconsistency.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 3, 6 (text). R grid over rounding intervals in R/p2210.R and inline check (max P under strict symmetry 0.0473). Card C007 read after judging; it frames this as no joint Wald solution; I consider the gap within method tolerance.
rows.rationale: Computed: SE from CI = (log 0.99 - log 0.43)/3.92 = 0.213; z = 1.95; P = 0.051 nominally; over rounding intervals with a symmetric CI, P in [0.0428, 0.0473]. The printed .048 is 0.0002-0.0007 outside the Wald range. Stata reports Wald CIs, but the adjusted model (age quartiles) could have been tested with a likelihood-ratio test; such differences of this size are expected. The other same-page tuples reproduce (adjusted death HR 0.81 [0.48-1.36], P = .43 vs printed .42). The result is borderline under any method and is labeled post hoc; I exclude it as not a reporting error.

rows.R: E changed to plan_material: the conflict is inside the plan. Protocol v1.5 §3.4 and §6.1 (pp. 11, 22) and the SAP §3.2 (p. 6) make FOBGold sensitivity the sole primary endpoint, with specificity and ROC AUC secondary; protocol §3.9 (pp. 13-14) and §7.2 (p. 28) call 'sensitivity and specificity ... and the AUC' of two FOBTs the primary endpoint. The article (pp. 1, 3) follows the SAP; AUC is disclosed as not reported.
rows.evidence: joi190039supp1 pp. 11, 13-14, 22, 28 (text); joi190039supp2 pp. 6, 8-9 (text); main pp. 1, 3-4 (text). Card C001 read after judging; it registers P_R by precedence; I classify by the material actually in conflict.
rows.rationale: The report's hierarchy (primary: sensitivity of the quantitative FIT at 2 cutoffs; secondary: specificity, PPV, NPV, qualitative test, sex-specific results; AUC and likelihood ratios 'not reported in this article') agrees with the protocol endpoint sections and the SAP. The broader wording in the protocol synopsis statistics paragraph and the sample-size section lists specificity and AUC with the primary endpoint, but the power calculation in §7.2 is for sensitivity alone (36% vs 60%, 90% power), so the intended primary endpoint is clear. I therefore treat this as an internal plan inconsistency of minor consequence. The secondary AUC analysis planned in the SAP (§5.5, pROC/DeLong) is not reported; this is disclosed in the article.

rows.R: Primary composite 211/989 vs 233/987: abstract, Table 3 (p. 9) and Figure 2 give 'risk ratio 0.93 (0.83-1.04)'; eFigure 12 (supp4 p. 42, rendered) lists the identical tuple as 'Odds Ratio (95% CI)' for the collapsed composite. Crude RR = 0.90 (0.77-1.06) and crude OR = 0.88, so 0.93 matches neither label.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 1, 4, 9 Table 3, 10 Figure 2 (rendered 170 dpi); joi190055supp4 p. 42 eFigure 12 (rendered 130 dpi); joi190055supp3 p. 2. R in R/p7505.R and inline. Card C001 read after judging; agrees on the label conflict; I add that neither label reproduces from the counts.
rows.rationale: Computed: RR = (211/989)/(233/987) = 0.904, log-Wald 95% CI 0.767-1.065; OR = (211/778)/(233/754) = 0.878. The printed headline value 0.93 (0.83-1.04) is called a risk ratio in the article and an odds ratio in the supplement and reproduces as neither. The uncorrected chi-square P = .226 matches the printed P = .23, so the counts and P agree while the effect estimate does not. This is the primary effect estimate quoted in the abstract, hence substantive with direct extraction impact (see also C004).

rows.R: Abstract (p. 1): hypoxemia 5.0% vs 13.6%, 'difference, -8.6% [95% CI, -11.1% to 6.1%]; P < .001'. Table 3 (p. 9): -8.6 (-11.1 to -6.1). Recomputed Wald CI for 49/989 vs 134/987: -11.2 to -6.1. The abstract upper limit has lost its minus sign.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 1, 9 Table 3 (rendered 170 dpi), 10-11 (text). R in R/p7505.R. Card C002 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: RD = 4.95% - 13.58% = -8.62%; SE = 0.0129; CI -11.15 to -6.09. As printed in the abstract, the interval would include 0, contradicting P < .001. Typographic sign error with the correct value in Table 3; minor, but the abstract is the most frequently extracted location.

rows.R: Protocol v2.6 (supp1 pp. 5, 12 §7.1.2) lists secondary endpoints including need for postoperative ventilatory support, hospital readmission within 30 days and mortality at day 90. The final SAP (supp3 p. 1, finalized January 2018 before database lock) and the article (p. 3) replace these with severe PPC, in-hospital mortality and others; 90-day mortality, ventilatory support and readmission are not reported. Article identifies the final SAP (p. 2).
rows.evidence: joi190055supp1 pp. 5, 12 (text); joi190055supp3 p. 1 (text); joi190055supp2 pp. 1-3 (text); main pp. 2-3, 9 Table 3; joi190055supp4 p. 21 §2.8 (text). Card C003 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The change is documented in a dated final SAP that precedes database lock and that the article cites, so the sequence is clear and the report follows the latest plan. Under the review rule that documented/disclosed changes remain differences, I retain it: the protocol's 90-day mortality window became in-hospital mortality, and two protocol secondary endpoints are not reported.

rows.R: The 'risk ratio' column (Table 3, Figure 2, eTable 8, eFigure 12) does not equal the ratio of group risks. For most rows it equals the high-PEEP risk divided by the pooled risk: pleural effusion 43/989 vs 21/987 crude RR 2.04, printed 1.35 (pooled-ratio 1.34); mortality 12 vs 5 crude 2.40, printed 1.41 (1.41); DIC 1 vs 0 printed 2.00 (2.00); ARDS 3 vs 1 crude 2.99, printed 1.50 (1.50).
rows.evidence: Main pp. 1, 4, 8-10 Table 3 and Figure 2 (rendered 170 dpi); joi190055supp4 p. 29 eTable 8, p. 42 eFigure 12 (rendered 130 dpi); joi190055supp3 p. 2. Systematic recomputation of 31 rows in R/p7505.R. Card C004 read after judging; agrees ('conditional-allocation diagnostic').
rows.rationale: For 31 Table 3 rows I computed crude RR, OR and p1/p_pooled = [e1/n1]/[(e1+e0)/(n1+n0)], which equals the share of events in the high-PEEP arm divided by its allocation share. Printed values match p1/p_pooled to 2 decimals in about 24 rows (e.g., cardiopulmonary edema 1.31, aspiration 1.33, pneumothorax 0.50, coma 0.99) and match the crude RR in none where the two differ; a few rows (primary 0.93, hypoxemia 0.51, hypotension 1.43) match neither. P values agree with chi-square tests on the counts. The methods state RRs by Wald approximation. Ratios are therefore shrunk toward 1 (e.g., hypotension crude 1.84 vs printed 1.43; hypoxemia 0.36 vs 0.51) and CIs are too narrow. All binary effect estimates in the trial report, including the abstract, are affected: substantive, direct.

rows.R: Final SAP (supp3 p. 2): Kaplan-Meier curves for time to PPC compared with log-rank tests. Article p. 4 and eFigure 8 (supp4 p. 38, rendered) give Kaplan-Meier curves with a Cox HR 0.88 (0.73-1.06), P = .190; no log-rank result is labeled anywhere. The Cox score test is asymptotically equivalent to log-rank, so the difference is small.
rows.evidence: joi190055supp3 pp. 2-3 (text); main pp. 4, 10-11 (text); joi190055supp4 pp. 30, 38, 42 (rendered). Card C005 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: The planned test is not reported as such; the time-to-event comparison is reported instead as a Cox HR with an unlabeled P. Inference would be practically identical, so I describe the difference as minor.

rows.R: Final SAP (supp3 p. 3) lists, among planned composite-outcome analyses, a GEE common-effect OR with a posteriori clinical severity weights. eTable 9 (supp4 p. 30) and eFigure 12 (p. 42) report random-effect, count, unweighted common-effect, interaction and average-relative-effect analyses, but no severity weights or weighted result.
rows.evidence: joi190055supp3 p. 3 (text); main pp. 4, 10-11 (text); joi190055supp4 pp. 30, 42 (rendered 130 dpi). Card C006 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: One of six planned composite-outcome sensitivity analyses is missing without explanation; the other five are reported. Because the weights were to be set a posteriori, omission removes the analysis that would address the clinical heterogeneity of the composite components (mild respiratory failure dominates the events).

rows.R: Table 2 (p. 7, rendered): tidal volume first hour 0.1 (0 to 0.2) P = .007, last hour 0.1 (0 to 0.2) P = .008, respiratory rate last hour -0.4 (-0.7 to 0) P = .02. From the printed means/SDs, e.g., SE = sqrt(1.5^2/989 + 0.4^2/987) = 0.049; P = .007 implies a difference of 0.13 with CI 0.04 to 0.23, which prints as '0 to 0.2'. Display rounding explains all three rows.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 4, 7 Table 2 (rendered PNG 170 dpi). Calculations in rationale. Card C007 read after judging; its rounding alternative is what I conclude.
rows.rationale: Tidal volume first hour: z = 2.70 for P = .007, so difference 0.133, CI 0.037 to 0.230, displayed 0.0 to 0.2. Last hour: with SD at its rounding bound (1.55) and n reduced by missing ventilation data (29 and 14 missing), P = .008 gives difference 0.142, CI 0.037 to 0.247, displayed 0 to 0.2. Respiratory rate: SE = sqrt(3.9^2/989 + 3.8^2/987) = 0.173; a difference of 0.389 gives CI -0.728 to -0.050 (displayed -0.7 to 0) and P = .025 (displayed .02). One-decimal display of a limit just inside zero produces the apparent conflict; no error.

rows.R: Table 2 (p. 8, rendered): monitoring 632/982 (64.9) and 651/984 (67.7); reversal 724/982 (74.3) and 723/984 (75.2). 632/982 = 64.4%, 651/984 = 66.2%, 724/982 = 73.7%, 723/984 = 73.5%. The printed percentages equal counts over the neuromuscular-blockade denominators 974/961 (64.9, 67.7, 74.3, 75.2), whereas the differences (-1.8, 0.2) use 982/984.
rows.evidence: Main p. 8 Table 2 (rendered PNG 170 dpi). R in R/p7505.R. Card C008 read after judging; agrees; the 974/961 denominator explanation is my addition.
rows.rationale: Computed: 632/974 = 64.89%, 651/961 = 67.74%, 724/974 = 74.33%, 723/961 = 75.23%, matching the printed percentages; differences with the printed denominators: 64.36 - 66.16 = -1.80 and 73.73 - 73.48 = 0.25, matching the printed differences. Within the same rows, percentages and differences therefore use different denominators. For reversal, the printed percentages imply -0.9 points while the printed difference is +0.2. Minor descriptive inconsistency.

rows.R: Table 3 (p. 9): disseminated intravascular coagulation 1 (0.1) vs 0, 'RR 2.00 (1.91 to 2.09)', P > .99. A CI excluding 1 is incompatible with P > .99 (Fisher P = 1.0), and a finite RR with a narrow CI is not estimable from 1 vs 0 events. 2.00 equals the high-PEEP risk over the pooled risk (see C004).
rows.evidence: Main pp. 9-10 Table 3 and notes b/c (rendered 170 dpi). R in R/p7505.R. Card C009 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: With 1 and 0 events, the crude RR is infinite and any sensible interval is extremely wide; the printed 1.91-2.09 interval and P > .99 contradict each other. The row illustrates the estimand problem in C004. With a single event the clinical consequence is negligible, so minor.

rows.R: Table 3 (p. 9): in-hospital mortality 12 (1.2) vs 5 (0.5), RR 1.41 (0.95 to 1.81), P = .09. On the log scale the interval is asymmetric (0.395 below vs 0.250 above the estimate) unlike neighboring rows, and it is far too narrow for 17 deaths: crude RR 2.40 (0.85-6.77). The P value matches an uncorrected chi-square test on the counts (.089); the estimate and interval do not.
rows.evidence: Main pp. 9-10 Table 3 (rendered 170 dpi). R in R/p7505.R and inline (crude RR CI). Card C010 read after judging; agrees on the asymmetry; I add the comparison with the crude RR.
rows.rationale: log(1.41) = 0.344, log(0.95) = -0.051, log(1.81) = 0.593: distances 0.395 and 0.250; other rows (e.g., pleural effusion 0.169/0.182) are near-symmetric. Crude RR = (12/989)/(5/987) = 2.40, SE(log) = 0.53, CI 0.85-6.77. Uncorrected chi-square P = 0.089 (printed .09), Yates 0.145, Fisher 0.142, so the P value reflects the counts while the printed 1.41 equals the high-PEEP/pooled risk ratio (C004). Mortality is a prespecified secondary safety outcome whose effect size and precision are misrepresented (the printed upper bound 1.81 vs about 6.8 from the counts): substantive.

rows.R: Protocol Appendix iii (supp1 p. 31): mild respiratory failure = PaO2 <60 mm Hg or SpO2 <90% on room air >=10 min but responding to supplemental O2; moderate = the same despite supplemental O2. eMethods §2.8 (supp4 p. 20) and Table 3 note d: mild = responding to O2 2 L/min; moderate = responding only to O2 >2 L/min. The mild/moderate boundary moves from response vs non-response to an oxygen-flow threshold.
rows.evidence: joi190055supp1 p. 31 (text); joi190055supp4 pp. 20-21 (text); joi190055supp3 p. 1; main pp. 9-10 Table 3 (rendered). Card C011 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Under the protocol, a patient hypoxemic on room air who responds to 4 L/min O2 is 'mild'; under the report's definition the same patient is 'moderate'. This matters for the secondary severe-PPC composite, which excludes only mild respiratory failure (116 vs 134 events), though not for the primary composite.

rows.R: Protocol extrapulmonary definitions (supp1 p. 32, rendered at 400 dpi): coma = Glasgow Coma Score <= 8 (underlined less-than sign; the text layer shows '<'). eMethods §2.8 (supp4 p. 21, rendered): coma = GCS < 8. Only a GCS of exactly 8 is classified differently; 2 vs 2 coma events.
rows.evidence: joi190055supp1 p. 32 (text layer plus 400-dpi crop showing the underlined symbol); joi190055supp4 p. 21 (300-dpi crop); main p. 9 Table 3. Card C012 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Boundary difference at GCS = 8 in a component of the extrapulmonary composite. The text layer of the protocol loses the underline, so the difference is visible only in the rendered page. Small practical effect (4 events total).

rows.R: eTable 8 per-protocol (supp4 p. 29, rendered): cardiopulmonary edema 15/917 vs 7/912, 'Effect estimate 1.36 (1.02-1.82)', P = 0.09. The interval excludes 1 while P > .05. Crude RR = 2.13 (0.87-5.20), uncorrected chi-square P = .089, matching the printed P; 1.36 equals the high-PEEP/pooled risk ratio (C004).
rows.evidence: joi190055supp4 p. 29 eTable 8 (rendered PNG 130 dpi); main p. 4 methods. R inline computation of RR CI and chi-square. Card C013 read after judging; agrees.
rows.rationale: Computed: RR = (15/917)/(7/912) = 2.13, log-Wald CI 0.87-5.20; chi-square without correction P = 0.089, with correction 0.137, Fisher 0.131. The printed estimate and interval come from a different (non-RR) quantity and imply statistical significance that the P value and the counts do not support. The interval as printed would lead a reader to conclude a significant per-protocol excess of cardiopulmonary edema with high PEEP.
